issues.legal_issue: A successful new allottee has discretion to adopt or decline existing coal-mining contracts made by a prior allottee, and a contract not adopted is not enforceable against the new allottee.
material_facts: A prior allottee had entered into a long-term arrangement with a mining contractor to develop a coal mine and supply coal.
After the earlier allocation was cancelled, the mine was allotted anew to a public power corporation.
The new allottee declined to continue the earlier mining arrangement and instead pursued competitive bidding.
issues.conclusion: The new allottee had complete discretion to decide whether to adopt or continue the prior contract. Because it declined to do so, the prior contractor could not require it to continue the contract; the contractor’s remedy lay against the prior allottee.
issues.legal_principle: Section 11(1) and (2) of the Coal Mines (Special Provisions) Act, 2015, gives the successful bidder or allottee the choice to adopt and continue a prior coal-mining contract; adoption creates a novation for the residual term or performance, while a contract not adopted ceases to be enforceable against the new allottee. Section 62 of the Contract Act, 1872, concerns the parties’ ability to agree to substitute, rescind or alter a contract. The Court applied the literal-interpretation principle stated in Jugalkishore Saraf v. Raw Cotton Company Limited, [1955] 1 SCR 1369, and noted the statutory context arising from Manohar Lal Sharma v. Principal Secretary, (2014) 9 SCC 516.

predicates.coal_mine_reallotted: A coal mine previously associated with a prior allottee was allotted to a new successful bidder or allottee.
predicates.prior_mining_contract_exists: A prior allottee had an existing contract with a third party relating to coal-mining operations.
predicates.new_allottee_declines_contract: The new successful bidder or allottee chose not to adopt or continue the existing contract.

issues.definition: When a coal mine is reallotted, an existing mining contract does not bind the new allottee if the new allottee declines to adopt it.

issues.legal_issue: A prior mining contractor’s investment and expectation of long-term continuation do not give it a right to compel a new allottee to continue the contract where the law gives the new allottee a choice and the public authority adopts a non-arbitrary policy change.
material_facts: The contractor had made substantial investments in machinery, roads and other infrastructure under an arrangement intended to last for a long term.
The mine was allotted anew to the public power corporation after the earlier allocation was cancelled.
The corporation chose to appoint a mine developer through competitive bidding and rejected the contractor’s request to continue.
The corporation’s stated reasons included seeking the best operator through competition and changed capital and revenue investment parameters.
issues.conclusion: The contractor had no vested right or legitimate expectation requiring the new allottee to continue the arrangement. A legitimate expectation could not fetter a non-arbitrary change of policy in the public interest.
issues.legal_principle: Section 11 of the Coal Mines (Special Provisions) Act, 2015, leaves adoption of prior contracts to the new allottee’s choice; substantial investment or reallocation of the same mine does not supply a right of continuation contrary to that choice. Under Kerala State Beverages (M and M) Corporation Limited v. P.P. Suresh, (2019) 9 SCC 710, freedom to change policy in the public interest is not fettered by substantive legitimate expectation so long as the government does not act arbitrarily or unreasonably. The Court also referred to Findlay, In re, 1985 AC 318.

predicates.claim_to_compel_contract_continuation: A prior contractor sought to require a new allottee to continue the earlier mining arrangement.
predicates.prior_contractor_made_substantial_invest: The prior contractor invested substantially in mining machinery, access roads or other infrastructure for the arrangement.
predicates.new_allottee_reallocated_mine: The mine was allotted anew to a public or other new allottee after the earlier allocation ended.
predicates.new_allottee_adopted_non_arbitrary_compe: The new allottee chose a competitive process for a stated operational or public-interest reason and the choice was not arbitrary or unreasonable.

issues.definition: A prior contractor’s substantial investment and claim to continuation do not compel continuation when the mine is newly allotted and the new allottee makes a non-arbitrary choice to use a competitive policy.

issues.legal_issue: Judicial review of a public authority’s decision on a representation concerns the legality and rationality of the decision-making process, not whether a court considers another outcome preferable.
material_facts: The contractor made a representation seeking continuation of its mining arrangement, and the public authority rejected it.
The authority relied on the aim of obtaining the best operator through competitive bidding and on changed capital and revenue investment parameters.
The authority followed the principles of natural justice, and reliance on a contractual bidding requirement was not the sole basis for its decision.
The High Court interfered with the authority’s decision and granted the contractor a first right of refusal.
issues.conclusion: The rejection of the representation was not shown to be illegal, procedurally improper or irrational under the applicable standard of review. The appeals were allowed, and the High Court’s judgment was set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Under Tata Cellular v. Union of India, (1994) 6 SCC 651, judicial review examines the decision-making process and is limited to legality, irrationality and procedural impropriety; it is not an appeal on the merits. Rashmi Metaliks Limited v. Kolkata Metropolitan Development Authority, (2013) 10 SCC 95, reaffirmed the authority of Tata Cellular. Irrationality is assessed by the Wednesbury standard: whether a properly directed and reasonable authority could have reached the decision. The Court applied these principles to the authority’s decision to pursue competitive bidding.

rule.if: challenge_to_administrative_decision and authority_followed_fair_process and authority_gave_rational_competitive_bidding_reasons and decision_not_illegal_or_irrational

predicates.challenge_to_administrative_decision: A party asked a court to review a public authority’s administrative decision rejecting its request.
predicates.authority_followed_fair_process: The authority considered the request after following the applicable principles of natural justice.
predicates.authority_gave_rational_competitive_bidd: The authority explained that competition could identify the best operator and referred to relevant changes in investment or bidding parameters.
predicates.decision_not_illegal_or_irrational: The authority acted within its powers, and its decision was not one that no reasonable authority could have reached.

issues.definition: A challenged administrative decision is not set aside when the authority followed a fair process, gave rational reasons for competition and did not act illegally or irrationally.
